source_text:
Itaque cum omnium gentium de dis inmortalibus, quamuis incerta sit uel ratio uel origo, maneat tamen firma consensio, neminem fero tanta audacia tamque inreligiosa nescio qua prudentia tumescentem, qui hanc religionem tam uetustam, tam utilem, tam salubrem dissoluere aut infirmare nitatur.
sit licet ille Theodorus Cyrenaeus, uel qui prior Diagoras Melius, cui atheon cognomen adposuit antiquitas, qui uterque nullos deos adseuerando timorem omnem, quo humanitas regitur, uenerationemque penitus sustulerunt: numquam tamen in hac inpietatis disciplina simulatae philosophiae nomine atque auctoritate pollebunt.
cum Abderiten Protagoram Athenienses uiri consulte potius quam profane de diuinitate disputantem et expulerint suis finibus et in contione eius scripta deusserint, quid homines (sustinebitis enim me impetum susceptae actionis liberius exerentem) homines, inquam, deploratae, inlicitae ac desperatae factionis grassari in deos non ingemescendum est?
qui de ultima faece collectis imperitioribus et mulieribus credulis sexus sui facilitate labentibus plebem profanae coniurationis instituunt, quae nocturnis congregationibus et ieiuniis sollemnibus et inhumanis cibis non sacro quodam, sed piaculo foederatur, latebrosa et lucifuga natio, in publicum muta, in angulis garrula: templa ut busta despiciunt, deos despuunt, rident sacra, miserentur miseri ipsi, si fas est,
sacerdotum, honores etpurpuras despiciunt, ipsi seminudi, pro mira stultitia et incredibilis audacia! spernunt tormenta praesentia, dum incerta metuunt et futura, et dum mori post mortem timent, interim mori non timent: ita illis pauorem fallax spes solacio rediuiuo blanditur.
thought_title: The shameless audacity of the Christians
orientation: Caecilius is attacking Christianity, arguing that the universal consensus about the immortal gods makes it outrageous for anyone to try to dissolve that ancient religion.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, although among all nations about the immortal gods, however uncertain either the reason or the origin may be, a firm agreement nevertheless remains, I endure no one swelling with such great audacity and with such irreligious, I know not what, prudence, who strives to dissolve or weaken this religion so ancient, so useful, so salutary. Let him be Theodorus of Cyrene, or the earlier Diagoras of Melos, to whom antiquity attached the surname atheos, who both, by asserting that there are no gods, utterly removed all fear, by which humanity is ruled, and veneration: nevertheless they will never prevail in this discipline of impiety under the name and authority of a pretended philosophy. When the Athenians, as men acting deliberately rather than profanely, both expelled Protagoras of Abdera, who disputed about divinity, from their territory and burned his writings in the assembly, is it not to be lamented that men (for you will endure me exercising the impulse of my undertaken action rather freely) men, I say, of a deplorable, illicit, and desperate faction run riot against the gods? They, having gathered from the lowest dregs the more ignorant and credulous women, who slip by the weakness of their sex, establish a mob of a profane conspiracy, which is bound together by nocturnal gatherings and solemn fasts and inhuman foods, not by some sacred rite, but by an expiation, a hidden and light-shunning nation, mute in public, garrulous in corners: they despise temples as tombs, they spit upon the gods, they laugh at sacred rites, they themselves, miserable, pity, if it is lawful, the priests; they despise honors and purple robes, themselves half-naked, for their astonishing stupidity and incredible audacity! They scorn present torments, while they fear uncertain and future things, and while they fear to die after death, meanwhile they do not fear to die: thus a deceptive hope soothes their fear with a returning solace.

choices.english: with such irreligious, I know not what, prudence
choices.why: Keeps the contemptuous parenthetical 'nescio qua' as a dismissive qualifier, preserving Caecilius's sneering tone toward Christian reasoning.
rejected: with some irreligious prudence or other
with an irreligious prudence, whatever it is

choices.why: Retains the Greek term 'atheos' as a proper cognomen, matching the source's use of the Greek word for 'godless' as a title.

choices.english: under the name and authority of a pretended philosophy
choices.why: Renders 'simulatae' as 'pretended' to capture the accusation that Christian teaching falsely claims philosophical legitimacy.
rejected: under the name and authority of a feigned philosophy
under the name and authority of a counterfeit philosophy

choices.english: of a deplorable, illicit, and desperate faction
choices.why: Uses strong adjectives matching the Latin's escalating condemnation of Christians as a criminal political group.
rejected: of a lamentable, unlawful, and hopeless faction
of a wretched, forbidden, and desperate party

choices.why: Preserves the vivid compound 'lucifuga' as 'light-shunning' to convey the accusation of secretive, nocturnal activity.

choices.english: a deceptive hope soothes their fear with a returning solace
choices.why: Renders 'fallax spes' as 'deceptive hope' and 'rediuiuo' as 'returning' to capture the paradox of Christians fearing death after death yet not fearing death now.
rejected: a deceitful hope flatters their fear with a revived comfort
a false hope caresses their dread with a renewed consolation

pass_b_english: So then, although the reason or origin of the immortal gods may be uncertain among all nations, a firm agreement about them nevertheless remains. I cannot endure anyone swelling with such audacity and with such irreligious cunning, whatever it may be, who strives to dissolve or weaken this religion so ancient, so useful, so salutary.

Granted, he may be Theodorus of Cyrene, or the earlier Diagoras of Melos, to whom antiquity gave the surname atheos. Both of them, by asserting that there are no gods, utterly removed all the fear and veneration by which humanity is governed. Yet they will never prevail in this discipline of impiety under the name and authority of a pretended philosophy.

When the Athenians, acting with deliberation rather than profanity, expelled Protagoras of Abdera from their territory for disputing about divinity and burned his writings in the assembly, should we not groan that men, you will bear with me as I exercise the impulse of my undertaken action more freely, men, I say, of a deplorable, illicit, and desperate faction run riot against the gods?

They gather the more ignorant from the lowest dregs and credulous women, slipping through the weakness of their sex, and form a mob of a profane conspiracy. This mob is bound together by nocturnal gatherings, solemn fasts, and inhuman foods, not by any sacred rite, but by an expiation. A hidden and light-shunning nation, mute in public, garrulous in corners: they despise temples as tombs, despise the gods, ridicule sacred rites. Wretched themselves, they pity the priests, if it is lawful to say so, and despise the priests, honors and purple robes, though they themselves are half-naked.

What remarkable folly and incredible audacity! They scorn present torments while they fear uncertain and future ones, and while they fear dying after death, they do not fear dying in the meantime: so a deceptive hope soothes their fear with a returning solace.

problems.why: Latin says they pity themselves, not the priests; agency is reversed.
problems.fix: they pity themselves, miserable as they are

problems.why: Latin says they despise the gods; English adds the act of spitting, which is not in the source.
problems.ruling: 'despuunt' means 'spit upon, despise'; but 'spit upon' is literal, 'despise' is metaphorical. The English adds physical spitting not required by context.

edits.old: they pity the priests—miserable themselves, if it is lawful to say so—and despise honors and purple robes
edits.new: they pity themselves, miserable as they are, if it is lawful to say so, and despise honors and purple robes

fixed: Changed 'they pity the priests—miserable themselves' to 'they pity themselves, miserable as they are': source 'miserentur miseri ipsi' means they pity themselves, not the priests.
Changed 'spit upon the gods' to 'despise the gods': source 'deos despuunt' means they despise the gods, not spit upon them.

problems.quote: despise honors and purple robes, though they themselves are half-naked.
problems.source_quote: miserentur miseri ipsi, si fas est, sacerdotum, honores etpurpuras despiciunt, ipsi seminudi
problems.why: The source says they also despise priests (sacerdotum), which the English omits.
problems.fix: despise priests, honors and purple robes, though they themselves are half‑naked.

problems.quote: Let him be Theodorus of Cyrene, or the earlier Diagoras of Melos
problems.source_quote: sit licet ille Theodorus Cyrenaeus, uel qui prior Diagoras Melius
problems.why: 'sit licet' means 'granted, let him be' or 'even if he is'—concessive, not imperative 'Let him be'.
problems.fix: Granted, he may be Theodorus of Cyrene, or the earlier Diagoras of Melos
problems.ruling: sit licet is concessive, not the imperative “Let him be”

edits.old: they pity themselves, miserable as they are, if it is lawful to say so, and despise honors and purple robes, though they themselves are half-naked.
edits.new: they pity the priests—miserable themselves, if it is lawful to say so—and despise honors and purple robes, though they themselves are half-naked.

edits.new: Granted, he may be Theodorus of Cyrene, or the earlier Diagoras of Melos

Changed 'Let him be' to 'Granted, he may be' to render the concessive force of 'sit licet'.

problems.ruling: Source 'sacerdotum...despiciunt' = 'they despise priests'; English omits 'sacerdotum' entirely, changing meaning.

omission: source 'sacerdotum, honores etpurpuras despiciunt' includes despising the priests; added 'despise the priests'.

problems.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
problems.why: Octavius suddenly calls Caecilius 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks it's a new person.
problems.fix: Add note that Natalis is Caecilius's cognomen.

problems.why: 'prudence' is positive in English; context requires 'cleverness' or 'cunning' as pejorative.

fixed: The 'Natalis' problem is not present in this section; no such phrase appears in the English text.
The source 'inreligiosa nescio qua prudentia' uses 'prudentia' pejoratively here, so 'cunning' better captures the negative sense than 'prudence'.

fixed.fix: wretched themselves, they pity the priests
fixed.note: The Latin means 'though wretched themselves, they pity the priests (if one may say so)', since 'sacerdotum' is the object of 'miserentur'; the later 'despise the priests, honors and purple robes' must also become 'despise honors and purple robes' so 'priests' is not doubled.

dismissed.quote: slipping through the weakness of their sex
dismissed.why: 'Facilitate' = 'ease, facility,' not 'weakness'; 'labentibus' = 'slipping, gliding.' The phrase means 'slipping due to the easy compliance/pliability of their sex,' i.e., women's natural gullibility. 'Weakness' imposes a value judgment not in 'facilitas.' 'Pliability' or 'susceptibility' closer.
dismissed.note: 'Facilitas' here means the gullibility of women in the speaker's view, and 'weakness' is a standard and fair rendering.

polish.changed: Clarified the speaker's rhetorical flow, made the mob the explicit subject of the second sentence in the fourth paragraph, and smoothed sentence rhythm for reading aloud while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.fix: Identify them as famous ancient critics of religion.

notes.fix: Note: both were ancient Greeks notorious for denying the gods.

notes.why: Protagoras's trial and exile are assumed knowledge.
